lessons.title: let, const, and var
lessons.explanation:
## Declaring variables

JavaScript has three ways to declare a variable — you will use two of them:

- `const` — the default. The binding cannot be reassigned.
- `let` — when you genuinely need to reassign.
- `var` — legacy; function-scoped and hoisted in confusing ways. Don't use it in new code.

### Worked example

```js
const price = 25;        // can never be reassigned
let quantity = 2;        // we expect this to change
quantity = 3;            // fine
// price = 30;           // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
const user = { name: 'Ada' };
user.name = 'Grace';     // fine! const freezes the BINDING, not the object
```

Line by line: `price` is bound once and forever. `quantity` is declared with `let` because we reassign it on the next line. The last two lines show the classic gotcha: `const` prevents **reassignment of the variable**, not **mutation of the value**. `user` still points at the same object; changing a property inside it is allowed.

### Common mistakes

- Using `let` everywhere "just in case". Default to `const`; it documents intent.
- Thinking `const` makes objects immutable. It doesn't — use `Object.freeze` if you need that.

lessons.title: Primitive Types & typeof
lessons.explanation:
## The seven primitives (and the one weird operator)

JavaScript values are either **primitives** or **objects**. The primitives: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `bigint`, `symbol`. Everything else — arrays, functions, plain objects — is an object.

`typeof` tells you what you're holding:

```js
typeof 'hi'        // 'string'
typeof 42          // 'number'
typeof true        // 'boolean'
typeof undefined   // 'undefined'
typeof null        // 'object'   ← famous historical bug, kept forever
typeof []          // 'object'   ← arrays are objects; use Array.isArray
typeof (() => {})  // 'function' ← the one non-primitive with its own typeof
```

### Worked example: a type guard

```js
function describe(value) {
  if (value === null) return 'null';          // check null FIRST
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return 'array';   // before typeof === 'object'
  return typeof value;
}
```

Order matters: `null` and arrays both report `'object'` from `typeof`, so you must test for them explicitly before falling back to `typeof`.

### Common mistakes

- `typeof x === 'null'` — never true. Compare `x === null` directly.
- Using `typeof` to detect arrays. Use `Array.isArray`.

lessons.title: Numbers, Math, and Floating Point
lessons.explanation:
## One number type (mostly)

JavaScript has a single `number` type: 64-bit IEEE-754 floating point. Integers and decimals are the same type, which is convenient right up until it isn't:

```js
0.1 + 0.2            // 0.30000000000000004
(0.1 + 0.2) === 0.3  // false!
```

### Worked example: money

Never store money as fractional dollars. Store **integer cents** and format at the edge:

```js
const priceCents = 1999;                      // $19.99
const total = priceCents * 3;                 // 5997 — exact
const display = (total / 100).toFixed(2);     // '59.97' — string for display
```

`toFixed(2)` returns a **string**, which is fine: by the time you format, you are done doing math.

### The toolbox

- `Math.round / floor / ceil` — nearest / down / up
- `Math.min(...arr)` / `Math.max(...arr)` — spread an array in
- `Math.abs`, `Math.trunc`, `n % m` (remainder, sign follows the left operand)
- `Number.parseInt(s, 10)`, `Number.parseFloat(s)`, `Number(s)` — string → number
- `Number.isInteger(n)`, `Number.isNaN(n)` — the safe checks

### Common mistakes

- `parseInt` without a radix on user input.
- Comparing floats with `===` after arithmetic. Compare against an epsilon, or work in integers.
- `NaN === NaN` is `false` — use `Number.isNaN`.

lessons.title: Strings & Template Literals
lessons.explanation:
## Strings

Strings are immutable: every "modification" produces a new string. Three quote styles — `'single'`, `"double"`, and `\`backticks\`` (template literals). Prefer template literals when interpolating:

```js
const name = 'Ada';
const greeting = `Hello, ${name}! You have ${2 + 3} messages.`;
// 'Hello, Ada! You have 5 messages.'
```

### The methods you will actually use

```js
'  hi  '.trim()                 // 'hi'
'abc'.toUpperCase()             // 'ABC'
'hello'.includes('ell')         // true
'hello'.slice(1, 3)             // 'el'   (end exclusive; negatives from the end)
'a,b,c'.split(',')              // ['a', 'b', 'c']
['a', 'b'].join(' - ')          // 'a - b'
'hello'.replaceAll('l', 'L')    // 'heLLo'
'7'.padStart(3, '0')            // '007'
'abc'.at(-1)                    // 'c'
```

### Worked example: a slug function

```js
function slugify(title) {
  return title
    .trim()                      // kill outer whitespace first
    .toLowerCase()               // normalize case
    .replaceAll(' ', '-');       // spaces → dashes
}
slugify('  Hello World  ')       // 'hello-world'
```

Each step returns a **new** string, so the calls chain naturally. Order matters: trim before replacing spaces, or the outer spaces become stray dashes.

### Common mistakes

- `str.replace('a', 'b')` only replaces the **first** occurrence — use `replaceAll`.
- Forgetting `slice`'s end index is exclusive.
- Comparing user input without `.trim().toLowerCase()` normalization.

lessons.title: Comparisons, Truthiness, ??, ||, &&
lessons.explanation:
## Strict equality and the truthy/falsy world

Always compare with `===` / `!==`. Loose `==` coerces types with rules nobody remembers (`'' == 0` is true!). The one idiomatic exception: `v == null` matches exactly `null` and `undefined`.

JavaScript treats every value as **truthy** or **falsy** when a condition needs a boolean. The complete falsy list is short — memorize it:

```js
false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN   // falsy
```

Everything else is truthy — including `'0'`, `'false'`, `[]`, and `{}`.

### Worked example: || vs ??

```js
const input = 0;
const a = input || 10;   // 10  — || replaces ANY falsy value
const b = input ?? 10;   // 0   — ?? replaces only null/undefined
```

Line by line: `input` is `0`, which is falsy. `||` sees a falsy left side and jumps to the fallback, destroying a perfectly valid zero. `??` (nullish coalescing) only falls back when the left side is `null` or `undefined`, so the real `0` survives. For "use a default when the value is missing", `??` is almost always what you mean.

`&&` short-circuits the other way: `a && b` evaluates to `a` if `a` is falsy, else `b`. That makes `user && user.name` a classic guard (today you'd write `user?.name`).

### Common mistakes

- Using `||` for defaults when `0` or `''` are legitimate values — use `??`.
- Thinking `[]` or `'0'` are falsy. Only the eight values above are falsy.
- `NaN === NaN` is false — use `Number.isNaN`.

lessons.title: if/else and Guard Clauses
for, while, for...of, break/continue
lessons.explanation:
## Repeating work

Three loops cover nearly everything:

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { ... }   // counted: you need the index
for (const item of items) { ... }     // iterate values: arrays, strings
while (condition) { ... }             // unknown iteration count
```

### Worked example: summing with for...of

```js
function sum(nums) {
  let total = 0;            // accumulator starts at the identity (0 for +)
  for (const n of nums) {   // visit each value; no index bookkeeping
    total += n;             // fold each value into the accumulator
  }
  return total;             // after the loop, the fold is complete
}
```

Line by line: the accumulator is declared with `let` **outside** the loop (inside, it would reset every pass). `for...of` hands you each element directly — no `i`, no off-by-one. Each iteration folds one value in, and the final value is returned after the loop ends.

### break and continue

- `break` exits the loop entirely — "found it, stop searching".
- `continue` skips to the next iteration — "not interested in this one".

```js
for (const u of users) {
  if (!u.active) continue;   // skip inactive users
  if (u.id === target) { found = u; break; }  // stop at first match
}
```

### Common mistakes

- `i <= arr.length` in a counted loop — one step too far, reads `undefined`.
- Declaring the accumulator inside the loop body, resetting it each pass.
- A `while` whose condition never changes — infinite loop.

Defaults, Rest, and Early Returns
lessons.explanation:
## Parameters in depth

A missing argument arrives as `undefined`. **Default parameters** replace exactly that:

```js
function greet(name = 'Guest', punct = '!') {
  return `Hello, ${name}${punct}`;
}
greet();              // 'Hello, Guest!'
greet('Ada');         // 'Hello, Ada!'
greet('Ada', '?');    // 'Hello, Ada?'
greet(undefined, '.') // 'Hello, Guest.'  — undefined triggers the default
greet(null);          // 'Hello, null!'   — null does NOT
```

Walk the calls: defaults fill in right-to-left as arguments run out. The fourth call shows the precise rule — only `undefined` (missing or explicit) triggers a default. `null` is a deliberate value and passes through.

### Rest parameters

`...nums` gathers "all remaining arguments" into a real array:

```js
function sum(...nums) {          // sum(1, 2, 3) → nums is [1, 2, 3]
  let total = 0;
  for (const n of nums) total += n;
  return total;
}
```

The rest parameter must come **last**, and there can be only one.

### Early returns

A function may have many `return` statements; the first one reached wins. Returning early for edge cases (the guard-clause pattern from control flow) keeps the main logic flat. A function that falls off the end without returning gives `undefined`.

### Common mistakes

- Expecting `null` to trigger a default — only `undefined` does.
- Putting a defaulted parameter before a required one: callers must pass `undefined` to skip it.
- Forgetting that `...rest` is a real array — you can loop it, index it, read `.length`.

lessons.title: Arrow Functions
lessons.explanation:
## The compact function syntax

```js
const double = (n) => n * 2;             // implicit return: no braces, no 'return'
const add = (a, b) => a + b;             // multiple params need parens
const greet = (name) => {                // braces = statement body:
  const msg = `Hi, ${name}`;            //   now 'return' is required
  return msg;
};
const toPair = (n) => ({ value: n });    // returning an object literal: wrap in parens!
```

Walk the forms: with **no braces**, the single expression after `=>` is returned automatically. Add braces and you have a normal body — forgetting `return` inside braces is the #1 arrow bug (the function silently returns `undefined`). The last line shows the object-literal trap: bare `{ value: n }` after `=>` parses as a code **block**, not an object, so the literal must be wrapped in parentheses.

### Where arrows shine: callbacks

```js
const prices = [100, 250, 40];
const doubled = prices.map((p) => p * 2);        // [200, 500, 80]
const cheap = prices.filter((p) => p < 150);     // [100, 40]
```

Inline, single-purpose, no name needed — exactly what array methods want. (Arrows also don't have their own `this`, which matters later with objects and classes; for pure functions it changes nothing.)

### Common mistakes

- `(n) => { n * 2 }` — braces without return: returns `undefined`.
- `(n) => { value: n }` — block, not object. Use `(n) => ({ value: n })`.
- Arrows are expressions: they are never hoisted, so define before use.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: Reassigning a `const` binding throws `TypeError: Assignment to constant variable` at runtime. It is not a parse-time syntax error, and it is never silently ignored in modules (which run in strict mode).

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.instructions:
Which line throws?
```js
const cart = [];
cart.push("apple");   // A
cart = ["banana"];    // B
```
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: `const` locks the *binding*, not the value. `push` mutates the array `cart` already points to — allowed. Line B rebinds `cart` to a new array — that reassignment throws.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: `score` starts at 10, is reassigned to 15, then `bonus` is computed from the *current* value of `score` (15 × 2 = 30). Reassignment replaces the value; later reads see the new one.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.instructions: Export a function `swap` that returns the two-element array `[b, a]` — the inputs swapped.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: Returning `[b, a]` builds a brand-new array whose first element is the second argument. No temporary variable is needed because the arguments are already independent bindings.
hints: Return a new array literal with the arguments in reverse order.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.instructions: Export a function `increment` that returns the number plus one.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: Numbers are passed by value, so `n + 1` computes a new number and returns it; the caller’s variable is untouched.
hints: One expression: the parameter plus one.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.instructions: Export a function `doubleThenAddTen` that doubles the number, then adds 10.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: Breaking the computation into a named `const` makes each step readable and gives the intermediate value a meaningful name. `(n * 2) + 10` in one line is equally correct.
hints: Store the doubled value in a `const`, then return it plus 10.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.instructions: This code throws when run. Fix it by changing **only the declarations** (keep the logic identical) so `nextLevel` computes correctly.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: `level` and `threshold` are both reassigned inside the loop, so they must be declared with `let`. The parameter `xp` is already reassignable. This is the practical rule: write `const`, and the moment you need to reassign, switch that one declaration to `let`.
hints: Which variables are *reassigned* inside the loop?
Any variable that gets a new value after declaration must be `let`, not `const`.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.instructions: Export a function `countDown(n)` that returns an array counting down from `n` to 1 (e.g. `countDown(3)` → `[3, 2, 1]`). Use a loop. For `n <= 0` return an empty array.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/variabl.explanation: The accumulator `result` is `const` (mutated, never reassigned) while the loop counter `i` is `let` inside the `for` head — each is the loosest declaration that still works. Looping from `n` down to 1 handles `n <= 0` for free: the condition is false immediately, so the empty array is returned.
hints: Start a `for` loop at `n` and decrement while `i >= 1`.
Declare the result array with `const` — you mutate it with push, never reassign it.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.explanation: `typeof null` returns `'object'` — a bug from JavaScript's first implementation that can never be fixed without breaking the web. Check for null with `value === null`.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.instructions: How do you reliably check that `v` is an array?
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.explanation: `typeof` reports `'object'` for arrays, so there is no `'array'` result. `Array.isArray(v)` is the standard, cross-realm-safe check.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.explanation: Strings, numbers and undefined report themselves. The surprises: `typeof null` is `'object'` (historical bug) and plain objects are also `'object'` — which is why null checks must come before object checks.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.instructions: Export a function `isString(v)` that returns `true` when `v` is a string primitive, else `false`. Use `typeof`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.explanation: `typeof` returns a *string*, so the check is a string comparison: `typeof v === 'string'`. The result of `===` is already a boolean, so you return the comparison directly — no if/else needed.
hints: Compare `typeof v` against the string `'string'`.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.explanation: `typeof` returns a *string*, so the check is a string comparison: `typeof v === 'undefined'`. The result of `===` is already a boolean, so you return the comparison directly — no if/else needed.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.instructions: Export `isMissing(v)` that returns `true` when `v` is either `null` **or** `undefined`, and `false` for everything else (including `0`, `""`, `false`, and `NaN`).

The idiomatic shortcut is `v == null`, the one place loose equality is conventionally accepted, because `==` considers `null` and `undefined` equal to each other and to nothing else — crucially NOT to `0`, `""`, or `false`.

Fun fact: `v == null` is the single case where `==` is idiomatic: it matches exactly null and undefined.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.instructions: Export `describe(v)` returning: `'null'` for null, `'array'` for arrays, otherwise whatever `typeof v` returns.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.explanation: The two values `typeof` lies about (null and arrays both say `'object'`) are peeled off first with precise checks; everything else is delegated to `typeof`. Guard-clause ordering like this — most specific first — is the standard shape for classification functions.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/primiti.instructions: Export `typeCensus(values)` that takes an array and returns an object counting values by `describe`-style type, e.g. `typeCensus([1, "a", null, 2])` → `{ number: 2, string: 1, null: 1 }`. Treat arrays as `"array"` and null as `"null"`.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation; their sum is 0.30000000000000004. For money, work in integer cents; for science, compare with a tolerance (epsilon).

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.instructions: Which expression reliably checks whether `x` is `NaN`?
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.explanation: NaN is the only JavaScript value not equal to itself, so `x === NaN` is always false. `Number.isNaN(x)` checks without coercion (unlike the global `isNaN`, which coerces strings first).

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.instructions: Export a function `centsToDisplay` that converts integer cents to a display string with two decimals, e.g. `1999` → `'19.99'`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.explanation: `toFixed(2)` pads and rounds to exactly two decimals and returns a string — ideal at the display edge. The arithmetic stays in integers until this final step, so no float drift can accumulate.
hints: Divide by 100, then `toFixed(2)`.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.instructions: Export a function `totalCents` that takes unit price in cents and a quantity, returns the exact total in cents.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.explanation: Because both operands are integers, the product is exact — IEEE-754 represents all integers up to 2⁵³ − 1 precisely. This is the whole argument for storing money in cents.
hints: Integer times integer is exact (within safe-integer range).

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.instructions: Export a function `clamp` that clamps `n` into the inclusive range `[min, max]` (args: n, min, max).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.explanation: `Math.max(min, n)` raises anything below the floor up to it; wrapping that in `Math.min(max, …)` caps anything above the ceiling. Clamp shows up everywhere: pagination bounds, volume sliders, scroll offsets.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.instructions: Export a function `average` that returns the mean of an array of numbers, and `0` for an empty array.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.explanation: The empty-array guard matters because `0 / 0` is `NaN` in JavaScript, not an exception — the bug would travel silently downstream. Guard first, then a simple sum-and-divide.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/values/numbers.instructions: Export a function `parseQuantity` that parses a string into a whole number with `Number.parseInt(s, 10)`; returns `1` if the result is `NaN` or less than 1, e.g. `'3'` → 3, `'abc'` → 1, `'-2'` → 1.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Which of these values is **falsy**?
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: The falsy values are exactly: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Empty arrays, empty objects, and the non-empty string `'0'` are all truthy — a classic source of bugs when checking form input.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: What is `'' == 0`, and what is `'' === 0`?
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Loose `==` coerces: the empty string converts to the number 0, so `'' == 0` is true. Strict `===` never coerces — different types means false immediately. This is exactly why you default to `===`.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: `0` and `""` are falsy but not nullish. `||` replaces both (printing 5 and anonymous), while `??` keeps both real values (printing 0 and the empty string, which shows as a blank line).
hints: || falls back on ANY falsy value; ?? only on null/undefined.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `isAdult` that returns `true` when `age` is 18 or more.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: A comparison already evaluates to a boolean, so you return it directly — `if (x) return true; else return false;` is always redundant.
hints: Return the comparison `age >= 18` directly.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `bothProvided` that returns `true` only when both `a` and `b` are neither `null` nor `undefined` (0 and "" count as provided).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: `x != null` is the one accepted use of loose inequality: it is true for every value except `null` and `undefined`, so `0` and `""` pass. Joining two checks with `&&` requires both to hold.
hints: The idiomatic nullish check is `x != null` — it matches exactly null and undefined.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `isFalsy` that returns `true` when `v` is falsy, `false` when truthy.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: `!v` coerces `v` to a boolean and negates it, so falsy values become `true`. (`!!v` is the companion idiom for "convert to boolean without flipping".)
hints: The `!` operator converts to boolean and flips it.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `withinRange` that returns `true` when `n` is in the inclusive range `[min, max]` (args: n, min, max).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Chained math notation like `1 <= n <= 10` parses as `(1 <= n) <= 10` — a boolean compared to 10, which is nonsense that silently "works". Two explicit comparisons joined with `&&` is the correct form.
hints: Two comparisons joined with && — JavaScript has no `min <= n <= max` syntax.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `sameValue` that returns `true` when `a` and `b` are strictly equal, treating `NaN` as equal to `NaN` (use `Number.isNaN` for that case).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: `NaN === NaN` is false — the one value not equal to itself — so it needs a special case before the general `===`. (This is exactly what the built-in `Object.is` does differently from `===`.)
hints: Handle the NaN pair first, then fall back to ===.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `toBoolean` that converts any value to `true`/`false` according to its truthiness (use double negation).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: `!v` produces a real boolean (the negation of truthiness); the second `!` flips it back, leaving truthiness itself as a boolean. `Boolean(v)` is the explicit spelling of the same thing.
hints: Negate twice: the first ! coerces and flips, the second flips back.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `eitherProvided` that returns `true` when at least one of `a`, `b` is neither `null` nor `undefined`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: `||` needs only one side to hold. Like `&&`, it short-circuits: if `a != null` is already true, the right side is never evaluated. De Morgan fans can also write `!(a == null && b == null)`.
hints: Same nullish checks as bothProvided, joined with || instead of &&.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export `displayName(name)` that returns `name` unless it is `null`, `undefined`, or an empty string — in those three cases return `'Guest'`. Note: `'0'` and `' '` (a space) are valid names.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: This is the mirror image of the ?? lesson: because the spec says empty string should ALSO fall back, `||` is the right tool — it replaces every falsy value. `' '` (a space) and `'0'` are truthy, so they pass through. Choose `||` vs `??` based on whether falsy-but-real values are valid.
hints: Which operator falls back on empty string as well as null/undefined?
Here `||` is actually correct, because '' should also become 'Guest'.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export `pageSize(config)` that returns `config.limit` unless it is `null` or `undefined`, in which case return `20`. A limit of `0` is valid and must be returned as-is.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Because `0` is a legitimate limit, `||` would be a bug here (`0 || 20` → 20). `??` only falls back on `null`/`undefined`: a missing property reads as `undefined`, so `{}` gets the default while `{ limit: 0 }` keeps its zero.
hints: `0` must survive — which operator ignores falsy and only reacts to nullish?

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export `firstChar(s)` that returns the first character of `s` when `s` is a non-empty string, and `''` (empty string) when `s` is `null`, `undefined`, or empty.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: `s && s[0]` short-circuits: if `s` is falsy (null, undefined, ''), the index never runs and the expression evaluates to `s` itself. The trailing `|| ''` converts whatever falsy value escaped into a clean empty string. An explicit `if` works too — the point is that `&&` never evaluates its right side when the left is falsy.
hints: `s && s[0]` only indexes when s is truthy.
Then `|| ''` normalizes any falsy result to the empty string.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions:
Export `normalizeField(value, fallback)`:
- If `value` is `null` or `undefined` → return `fallback`.
- If `value` is a string → return it trimmed; if the trimmed result is empty, return `fallback`.
- Otherwise (numbers, booleans, etc.) → return `value` unchanged — including `0` and `false`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: This combines every tool from the lesson: the `== null` nullish check first, a `typeof` branch for strings, and a deliberate `||` where empty-string-falls-back is the spec. The crucial subtlety is that `0` and `false` must NOT be replaced — which is why the function cannot simply be `value || fallback`.
hints: Three cases in order: nullish, string, everything else.
`value == null` catches both null and undefined in one check.
After trimming, `trimmed || fallback` is safe because an empty trimmed string SHOULD fall back.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: The first true branch wins: 95 ≥ 70, so it returns 'C' and never reaches the other checks. Overlapping range checks must be ordered most-specific (highest threshold) first.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: 15 is not > 25, so the first branch is skipped; 15 > 10, so 'mild' prints and the else is skipped. Code after the whole if/else chain always runs, so 'done' prints too.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `signOf` that returns `'positive'`, `'negative'`, or `'zero'` for a number.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Because each branch returns, no `else` is needed — if execution reaches the last line, both earlier conditions must have been false, so the value is zero. This flat early-return chain is the house style for classification.
hints: Three mutually exclusive cases: two ifs and a final return.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `letterGrade` that returns `'A'` for 90+, `'B'` for 80–89, `'C'` for 70–79, `'F'` below 70.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Ordering thresholds highest-first means each later check only sees scores that already failed the earlier ones, so `score >= 80` really means "between 80 and 89" without writing the upper bound.
hints: Check the highest threshold first and return immediately.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `shippingCost` that returns shipping in cents: free (0) for subtotals of 5000+ cents, 499 for 2000–4999, else 999.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Tiered pricing is the letter-grade pattern wearing a business suit: thresholds descend, first match returns. Keeping money in integer cents (from the numbers lesson) avoids float drift in the comparisons.
hints: Same highest-first tier pattern as letter grades, with cents.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `maxOfThree` that returns the largest of three numbers WITHOUT using Math.max.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: The running-champion pattern: assume the first value is the max, then let each contender overwrite it if bigger. It scales to any number of values (it is how you max over an array with a loop) where nested comparisons would explode.
hints: Start with the first value as the champion; challenge it with each other value.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `isLeapYear` that returns `true` for leap years: divisible by 4, except centuries (divisible by 100) unless also divisible by 400.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: The three rules overlap (2000 is divisible by all three), so order resolves the conflict: most specific exception first. `% n === 0` is the standard divisibility test.
hints: Check the most specific rule (400) first, then 100, then 4.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `absValue` that returns the absolute value of a number WITHOUT using Math.abs.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: One guard clause handles the only case that needs work: negating a negative (`-n`) makes it positive. Zero and positives fall through untouched — no else required.
hints: Negative numbers get flipped with unary minus; everything else passes through.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `ticketPrice` that returns the ticket price in cents by age: under 5 → 0, 5–17 → 800, 18–64 → 1500, 65+ → 1000.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: The mirror of highest-first: ascending upper bounds work because each check only sees ages that failed the earlier (lower) ones, so `age < 18` effectively means "5 to 17". Either direction is fine — just be consistent and let the order carry the lower bound implicitly.
hints: Ascending upper bounds this time: each check rules out everything below it.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export a function `minOfThree` that returns the smallest of three numbers WITHOUT using Math.min.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Identical structure to maxOfThree with the comparison flipped. Recognizing that min/max/longest/newest are all the same running-champion pattern with a different comparison is a real level-up moment.
hints: Running champion again — but challengers win by being SMALLER.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions:
Export `discountPercent(user)` using guard clauses:
- if `user` is `null`/`undefined` → return `0`
- if `user.banned` is truthy → return `0`
- if `user.years >= 5` → return `20`
- if `user.years >= 1` → return `10`
- otherwise → return `5`
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Guards must run in dependency order: checking `user.banned` before confirming `user` exists would throw a TypeError on null. After the rejections, the tiers run highest-first like any range chain. Five rules, five lines, zero nesting.
hints: One guard per rule, in the order given, each returning immediately.
The null guard MUST come first or `user.banned` throws on null.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions: Export `classify(n)`: return `'both'` if `n` is divisible by 3 and 5, `'three'` if only by 3, `'five'` if only by 5, else `'neither'`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: The combined condition must be tested before either single condition, because 15 satisfies all three checks and only the first true branch runs. This check-the-intersection-first ordering is the heart of FizzBuzz and of every overlapping-rules problem.
hints: Why must the "both" check come first?
15 is divisible by 3, so a bare `% 3` check first would steal it.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.instructions:
Export `validateRegistration(form)` where `form` is `{ username, password, age }`.
Return the FIRST applicable error string, or `null` if valid:
- `'username required'` — username missing (nullish) or empty/whitespace-only
- `'username too short'` — fewer than 3 characters after trimming
- `'password too short'` — password is nullish or shorter than 8 characters
- `'must be 13 or older'` — age is below 13
Use guard clauses; the happy path returns `null`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/c.explanation: Real-world validation in miniature: normalize first (`?? ""` turns nullish into a trimmable string), then one guard per rule in spec order so "first error wins" falls out naturally. Checking `form.password == null` before `.length` prevents a TypeError — reading properties of undefined is the most common crash in form handlers.
hints: Normalize the username once at the top: `(form.username ?? "").trim()`.
Each rule is one guard clause returning its error string.
Password may be missing entirely — check nullish before reading .length.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Inside a loop over orders, you want to **skip** cancelled orders but **stop entirely** at the first refunded one. Which pair?
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: `continue` abandons only the current iteration (skip this one, keep looping); `break` abandons the whole loop (stop searching). Skip → continue, stop → break.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: The loop visits 1, 2, 3, 4. When i is 3, `continue` jumps straight to i++, skipping both the addition and the log. So 1, 2 and 4 are added (total 7) and three 'added' lines print.
hints: i runs 1,2,3,4 — which iteration does continue skip?

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `sumTo` that returns the sum 1 + 2 + … + n (and 0 when n < 1).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: The accumulator lives outside the loop so it survives across iterations. When n < 1 the condition `i <= n` is false immediately and the initial 0 is returned — the edge case costs nothing.
hints: Counted loop from 1 to n inclusive, accumulating into a `let`.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `countVowels` that counts the vowels (a, e, i, o, u — lower-case input) in a string.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: Strings are iterable, so `for...of` yields each character. Using `'aeiou'.includes(ch)` as the membership test avoids a five-way `||` chain — the vowels string acts as a tiny lookup set.
hints: for...of over the string; check membership with a string includes.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `repeatWord` that returns `word` repeated `n` times separated by single spaces (empty string for n <= 0), e.g. `("go", 3)` → `"go go go"`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: Building an array and joining once sidesteps the trailing-separator problem that plagues string concatenation in a loop ('go go go ' with a stray space). Collect-then-join is the idiomatic shape.
hints: Collect n copies into an array, then join with a space.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `firstNegative` that returns the first negative number in the array, or `null` if there is none — stop looping as soon as it is found.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: Returning from inside a loop exits both the loop and the function at once — the cleanest form of early exit for search loops. The `return null` after the loop only runs when nothing matched.
hints: Return directly from inside the loop — that stops it even harder than break.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `doublingSteps` that returns how many times you must double `start` (positive) before it reaches at least `target` — e.g. `(1, 8)` → 3, and 0 if start is already >= target.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: The iteration count depends on the data, which is the signature of a `while` problem. The loop body must change something the condition reads (`value`), or it never terminates — the number-one while-loop bug.
hints: You cannot know the iteration count up front — that is what while is for.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `sumUntilLimit` that sums array values left to right but STOPS (break) before adding any value that would push the total above `limit`; returns the total so far (args: nums, limit).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: The guard checks `total + n` — the hypothetical next state — before mutating, so the loop never overshoots. Check-then-commit ordering like this is exactly how budget caps, rate limits and pagination cutoffs are written.
hints: Test the WOULD-BE total before committing the addition.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `factorial` that returns n! (the product 1 × 2 × … × n) using a loop; `factorial(0)` is 1.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: The accumulator starts at the identity for the operation: 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication. Starting the loop at 2 skips a useless ×1, and n of 0 or 1 never enters the loop, returning the identity — which is exactly the mathematical definition.
hints: Like sumTo, but multiply — and the accumulator starts at 1, not 0.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `sumDigits` that returns the sum of the decimal digits of a non-negative integer, e.g. `493` → 16 — use a while loop with `% 10` and `Math.floor(n / 10)`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: Each pass extracts the last digit with remainder-10 and shrinks the number with integer division, so the loop provably terminates. Digit-peeling with % and floor-divide is a classic numeric-loop idiom worth owning.
hints: `n % 10` peels the last digit; flooring n/10 drops it.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export a function `containsValue` that returns `true` if the array contains `target` (use a loop and ===, not .includes) (args: arr, target).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: The true case can be decided early (first match), but the false case requires the whole array to have been checked — which is why `return false` must live AFTER the loop, never inside an else.
hints: Return true from inside the loop; false only after checking everything.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export `maxIn(nums)` returning the largest number in a non-empty array using a loop (no `Math.max`). Works with all-negative arrays.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: Seeding the champion with the first element (not 0) is what makes all-negative arrays work: `[-5, -2, -9]` never exceeds 0, so a zero-seeded max would wrongly return 0. Seed from the data, then challenge with each element.
hints: Start the champion at nums[0], NOT at 0 — why does 0 break?
An all-negative array never beats a starting champion of 0.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions: Export `evenCountdown(n)` returning an array of the even numbers from `n` down to 2 inclusive, e.g. `evenCountdown(7)` → `[6, 4, 2]`. Return `[]` for n < 2.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: A descending counted loop plus a parity filter. The accumulator array is `const` (mutated via push, never reassigned). Stepping `i -= 2` from the nearest even number is a fine optimization, but filter-inside-loop reads more clearly at this stage.
hints: Loop downward with i-- and keep only `i % 2 === 0`.
Alternative: start at the largest even ≤ n and step by -2.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.instructions:
Export `fizzBuzz(n)` returning an array of length `n` for the numbers 1..n where each entry is:
- `'FizzBuzz'` if divisible by both 3 and 5
- `'Fizz'` if divisible by 3 only
- `'Buzz'` if divisible by 5 only
- otherwise the number itself (as a number, not a string)
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/l.explanation: FizzBuzz fuses the lesson: a counted loop, the check-the-intersection-first rule from conditionals (15 before 3 or 5), and an accumulator array. The subtle requirement — plain numbers in the default branch — is why the test uses strictEqual: `"1"` would fail where `1` passes.
hints: Loop 1..n; classify each i; push the result.
The both-divisible case must be checked first (divisible by 15).
Push the raw number i in the default case — not String(i).

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: No `break` statements, so after matching `case 'b'` execution falls through into `case 'c'` and reassigns `out` to 'C'. Every non-returning case needs a `break` unless fall-through is deliberate.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: The first ternary picks 'sold out' because 0 > 0 is false. The second sits inside a template literal — legal because a ternary is an expression — and picks the singular 'file' for n === 1.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `statusText` that maps an HTTP code with a switch: 200 → `'OK'`, 201 → `'Created'`, 404 → `'Not Found'`, 500 → `'Server Error'`, anything else → `'Unknown'`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: When every case returns, no breaks are needed — the return exits the whole function before fall-through can happen. Fixed value→value mappings like this are exactly what switch (or a lookup object) is for.
hints: One case per code, each returning; default handles the rest.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `dayType` that returns `'weekend'` for `'sat'`/`'sun'` and `'weekday'` for `'mon'`–`'fri'` using deliberate case fall-through, `'invalid'` otherwise.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: Stacked empty cases are the one legitimate fall-through: several labels funnel into one body. The alternative — repeating the body five times — is noise. The default case keeps bad input from silently returning undefined.
hints: Stack the cases that share an answer directly on top of each other.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `seasonOf` that maps month number (1-12) to season with stacked cases: 12,1,2 → `'winter'`; 3,4,5 → `'spring'`; 6,7,8 → `'summer'`; 9,10,11 → `'fall'`; other → `'invalid'`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: Grouped fall-through scales: twelve inputs collapse into four bodies. Note winter wraps around the year boundary (12, 1, 2) — a range check like month <= 2 would need an awkward || for December, but stacked cases handle it flatly.
hints: Four groups of three stacked cases each.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `pluralize` that returns `count + ' ' + word`, adding `'s'` to the word unless count is exactly 1 — use a ternary. e.g. `(1, 'file')` → `'1 file'`, `(3, 'file')` → `'3 files'`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: Because a ternary is an expression, the singular/plural choice embeds directly in the concatenation — no temporary variable, no if/else block. Note 0 takes the plural ('0 items'), so the test is `=== 1`, not `< 2`.
hints: The ternary picks between word and word + "s" inline.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `parityLabel` that returns `'even'` or `'odd'` for an integer using a single ternary (negative numbers too: -3 is odd).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: JavaScript remainder keeps the sign of the left operand, so `-3 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`. Comparing against 0 (`% 2 === 0`) is safe for both signs, where `n % 2 === 1` would misreport every negative odd number.
hints: Test `n % 2 === 0` — comparing to 0 dodges the negative-remainder trap.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `gradePoints` that maps a letter grade to GPA points with a switch: `'A'` → 4, `'B'` → 3, `'C'` → 2, `'D'` → 1, anything else → 0.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: F and invalid input share the answer 0, so both route through `default`. When a legitimate value and the error fallback coincide, merging them into default keeps the switch minimal — just make sure that is truly the intended behavior.
hints: F needs no case of its own — let default absorb it.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `yesNo` that converts a boolean to the string `'yes'` or `'no'` with a ternary.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: Writing `b === true ? …` is redundant: `b` is already a boolean and the ternary consumes it directly. Boolean-to-label conversion is the smallest possible ternary and a very common display helper.
hints: The boolean IS the condition — no comparison needed.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export a function `absTernary` that returns the absolute value of `n` as a single ternary expression (no Math.abs, no if).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: The ternary expresses choose-a-value logic in one expression: flip negatives, pass everything else. Comparing this to the earlier if-version of abs shows exactly what ternaries are for — value selection, not control flow.
hints: Same logic as the if-based absValue, compressed into one expression.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export `nextAction(light)` with a switch: `'green'` → `'go'`, `'yellow'` → `'slow'`, `'red'` → `'stop'`. For any other input return `'stop'` (fail safe).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: Because unknown input must behave like 'red', the red case can merge into `default` — the safest state is the fallback, so an unrecognized light can never cause a 'go'. Designing the default to be the safe outcome is a small instance of fail-safe design.
hints: Notice 'red' and unknown inputs share the same answer…
Let default cover both — fewer cases, fail-safe by construction.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.instructions: Export `tempLabel(c)` using a single return with (at most) two chained ternaries: below 0 → `'freezing'`, 0 to 25 inclusive → `'mild'`, above 25 → `'hot'`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: A chained ternary reads top-to-bottom like an if/else-if chain when formatted as `cond1 ? v1 : cond2 ? v2 : v3`. Two levels is the readability ceiling — this exercise is also a calibration point for when to STOP using ternaries and reach for if/else.

- An unknown operator returns `null`.
Use a switch.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/control-flow/s.explanation: The switch dispatches on the operator string; each case returns, so no breaks. The interesting case is division: JavaScript happily evaluates `5 / 0` to `Infinity` without throwing, so the zero check must be explicit — a ternary inside the case keeps it compact. Unknown operators fall to `default`, the same null-for-invalid contract.
hints: One case per operator, each returning its expression.
The division case needs a guard — a ternary inside the case works.
In raw JS, 5 / 0 is Infinity, not an error — you must check b yourself.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/decl.instructions: This function logs the answer instead of returning it, so callers always get `undefined`. Fix it so the computed value is RETURNED (remove the console.log).

hints: A function with no return statement returns undefined.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/decl.instructions: Export `applyTwice(fn, x)` that calls the function `fn` on `x`, then calls it again on the result, and returns that: `applyTwice(double, 3)` → `12`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/decl.explanation: The parameter `fn` holds a function value, so `fn(x)` calls it; nesting `fn(fn(x))` feeds the first result into the second call. Taking functions as arguments is the foundation under map, filter, and every event handler you will ever register.
hints: `fn` is already a function — call it like any other: fn(x).
Nest the calls: the inner result feeds the outer call.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/decl.instructions:
Export `makeOps()` that returns an object with three function properties:
- `add(a, b)` → a + b
- `sub(a, b)` → a − b
- `best(a, b)` → the larger of a and b
Also export `runOp(ops, name, a, b)` that looks up `ops[name]` and calls it with `(a, b)`, returning `null` if no such operation exists.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/decl.explanation: An object whose values are functions is a dispatch table — the data-driven alternative to a switch. `ops[name]` retrieves the function value; the typeof guard turns a bad name into a clean `null` instead of a "fn is not a function" crash. This pattern powers routers, command handlers and reducers.
hints: Function expressions can be object property values.
In runOp, `ops[name]` fetches the function (bracket access with a variable key).
Validate with `typeof fn !== "function"` before calling.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Given `function f(x = 10) { return x; }` — what are `f()`, `f(undefined)`, and `f(null)`?
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: Defaults trigger on `undefined` only — both the missing argument and the explicit `undefined`. `null` is treated as a real, intentional value and is returned as-is. This asymmetry is the same one `??` honors.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `greetUser` that returns `'Hello, NAME!'`, defaulting the name to `'Guest'` when no argument (or undefined) is passed.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: The default lives in the signature, so the body never worries about missing input. This is cleaner than `name = name || "Guest"` inside the body, which would also clobber legitimate falsy values.
hints: Put the fallback in the parameter list: name = "Guest".

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `power` that returns `base` raised to `exponent`, with the exponent defaulting to 2.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: Defaulting the LAST parameter is the ergonomic order: the common call `power(3)` just omits it. `**` is the exponentiation operator (Math.pow in older code).
hints: The ** operator does exponentiation; default the second parameter.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `sumAll` that accepts ANY number of numeric arguments (rest parameter) and returns their sum; zero arguments → 0.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: The rest parameter turns a variable-length call into a fixed problem: an array to fold. With no arguments, `nums` is simply `[]` and the accumulator comes back untouched — the edge case handles itself.
hints: Gather with ...nums, then loop the array.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `countArgs` that returns how many arguments it was called with (use a rest parameter).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: `...args` is a genuine array, so `.length` answers the question directly. Note that `null` still counts as one argument — rest counts positions, not truthiness.
hints: Rest gathers into an array; arrays have .length.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `longestWord` that accepts any number of string arguments (rest) and returns the longest one (first wins ties); no arguments → empty string.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: Rest + running champion: the comparison is strictly `>` so an equal-length later word cannot dethrone the earlier one — that single character is what implements "first wins ties".
hints: Running champion over the rest array, comparing .length.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `joinWords` that accepts a separator as the FIRST argument and any number of words after it (rest), returning the words joined by the separator.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: Fixed parameters and a rest parameter coexist: `sep` claims the first argument, rest sweeps up everything after. Since rest is a real array, `.join` finishes the job in one call.
hints: Normal parameter first, rest parameter after.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `finalPrice` that returns `price × (1 + taxRate) − discount`, where taxRate defaults to 0.25 and discount defaults to 0.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: Defaults stack left to right: `finalPrice(100)` uses both, `finalPrice(100, 0.5)` overrides only the first. To override just the discount you would pass `undefined` for the rate — which is why the most-commonly-overridden default should sit leftmost among the defaults.
hints: Two defaulted parameters after the required one.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `maxOf` that accepts any number of numeric arguments and returns the largest; with no arguments return `null`.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: The empty-call guard must come first: there is no honest maximum of nothing (`Math.max()` returns -Infinity, which is rarely what anyone wants). Seeding from the data keeps all-negative inputs correct, as in the loops lesson.
hints: Guard the empty call, seed the champion from nums[0].

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export a function `clampTo` that clamps `n` into [min, max] where min defaults to 0 and max defaults to 100.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: Defaults encode the common case (percent-style 0-100) while keeping the general form reachable. The clamp itself is the min-of-max sandwich from the numbers lesson — tools composing across lessons.
hints: Same clamp as before, but the bounds have defaults.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export `fullName(first, last, middle)` returning `'First Middle Last'` when a middle name is given and `'First Last'` otherwise (middle missing or undefined).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: An unpassed parameter is `undefined`, which the early return detects — one branch per shape, each returning its own template. Note the optional parameter goes LAST in the signature even though it appears in the middle of the output; parameter order serves the caller, not the output format.
hints: A parameter that was never passed holds undefined.
Guard on `middle === undefined`, return early.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export `safeDivide(a, b)` that returns `a / b`, but returns `null` early when `b` is `0` (checked first, as a guard clause).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: The guard converts the one dangerous input into an explicit sentinel (`null`) before the happy path runs. Dividing zero BY something is fine (`0 / 5` is 0) — only a zero divisor is guarded, which the test for `(0, 5)` confirms.
hints: Guard first, divide second.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions: Export `avgOf(...nums)` returning the mean of all numeric arguments, or `0` when called with none.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: Rest + guard + fold: the empty-call guard prevents `0 / 0` → `NaN` from leaking out silently. The rest array makes "any number of arguments" the same problem as "an array of numbers" — one mental model for both.
hints: Guard the empty case (0/0 is NaN!), then sum and divide.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.instructions:
Export `buildUrl(base, path = '', ...segments)`:
- Start from `base` with any trailing `/` removed.
- If `path` is non-empty, append `'/' + path`.
- Append `'/' + segment` for each extra segment.
- `buildUrl('https://api.dev/', 'users', '42', 'posts')` → `'https://api.dev/users/42/posts'`
- `buildUrl('https://api.dev')` → `'https://api.dev'`
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/para.explanation: All three parameter tools in one signature: a required base, a defaulted path (so `buildUrl(base)` works without undefined leaking into the string), and a rest parameter for open-ended segments. Normalizing the trailing slash FIRST means every append can safely add its own `/` — fixing the joint once instead of special-casing every append.
hints: endsWith("/") + slice(0, -1) normalizes the base.
The default path of "" makes the no-path call safe to check with !==.
Loop the rest array, appending "/" + segment each time.


The accumulation loop threads `result` through each step, so order matters (the tests prove `+1 then ×2` differs from `×2 then +1`). This is function composition — the idea under middleware chains and data pipelines.

Inside, loop over fns, threading the value through each call.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.instructions: Export `makeAdder` that returns a function: `makeAdder(5)` gives a function that adds 5 to its argument. The returned function must keep its state/configuration in a closure.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.instructions: Export `makeGreeter` that returns a function: `makeGreeter('Hi')` gives a function so that calling it with `'Ada'` returns `'Hi, Ada!'`. The returned function must keep its state/configuration in a closure.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.instructions: Export `makeToggle` that returns a function that alternates between `true` and `false`, starting with `true` on the first call. The returned function must keep its state/configuration in a closure.

Start it at false so the first flip returns true.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.instructions: Export `sumPositive(nums)` that sums only the positive numbers in the array. Careful: declare the accumulator ONCE, outside the loop — declaring it inside would reset it every iteration.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.explanation: Scope placement is the whole exercise: `total` must live in the function body (surviving all iterations) while `n` is fresh per iteration. Putting `let total = 0` inside the loop body is the classic scope bug — every pass would shadow… actually re-create it, and the function would return just the last positive number checked, or 0.
hints: The accumulator belongs in the function scope; the loop variable in the loop scope.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.instructions: This function should collect names of items that are in stock, but it always returns an empty array. The bug: an inner declaration shadows the outer `found`. Fix it (change ONE line).
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.explanation: The stray `let` turned an assignment into a declaration, creating a block-local `found` that vanished at the closing brace while the outer array stayed empty. Deleting `let` makes the line reach the outer binding. When a variable mysteriously "never updates", look for an accidental redeclaration shadowing it.
hints: The inner `let found` declares a NEW variable that dies at the end of the if-block.
Remove the `let` so the line assigns to the outer variable instead.

bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.instructions:
Export `makeAccount(initial)` returning an object with three function properties sharing ONE private balance:
- `deposit(amount)` — adds amount (ignore amounts <= 0), returns the new balance
- `withdraw(amount)` — subtracts amount and returns the new balance, but returns `null` (balance unchanged) if amount <= 0 or exceeds the balance
- `getBalance()` — returns the current balance
The balance must NOT be a property on the returned object — it lives only in the closure.
bootforge/js-fundamentals/functions/scop.explanation: Three functions returned in one object all close over the same `balance`, so they share state while the outside world cannot touch it — the privacy test (`acc.balance` is undefined) proves the data lives in the closure, not on the object. The validate-before-mutate rule in withdraw keeps the account consistent even on rejected operations. This is the module/encapsulation pattern closures were made for.
hints: Declare `let balance = initial` then return an object of functions.
All three functions close over the SAME balance variable.
withdraw validates before mutating — return null without touching balance.
